h1: Using Irish moss and kettle finings for clearer homebrew
title: Irish Moss and Kettle Finings | Craft Beer School
desc: How Irish moss and carrageenan tablets clear homebrew in the kettle: what they do, when and how much to add plus what they cannot fix.
teaser: A teaspoon of Irish moss in the last 15 minutes of the boil gives clearer wort and clearer beer. Here is how it works.
standfirst: Kettle finings help proteins clump and drop out of wort before it reaches the fermenter. They cost little and add only one step to the boil. Here is how we use them and what they will not fix.
sections:
Wort carries proteins and polyphenols from the malt and hops. As wort boils and then cools, these bind together and form particles. Large particles settle out as trub. Small ones stay in suspension, cloud the wort and later cause haze in the beer, especially when it is chilled.

Kettle finings help those particles grow big enough to fall out. The common ones come from red seaweed. Irish moss is the dried seaweed itself. Refined tablets contain carrageenan, the active compound extracted from it. Carrageenan carries a negative charge. Haze-forming proteins carry a positive charge at wort pH. The two attract, form larger flocs and drop to the bottom of the kettle.

• Irish moss is flaked, dried seaweed. It is cheap and keeps well. Rehydrate it in a little warm water for 15 to 30 minutes before adding so it disperses evenly. A common dose is about a teaspoon for a 20 litre batch.
  • Carrageenan tablets are more concentrated and more consistent. A typical dose is one tablet per batch of around 20 litres, crushed or dropped in whole as the maker directs.

Both do the same job. Tablets give more predictable results. Irish moss suits brewers who want a single packet that lasts a year.

Store either kind sealed and dry. In a humid Indian monsoon, an open packet of Irish moss can pick up moisture and grow mould. A small airtight jar in a cupboard keeps it usable for a long time.

Add kettle finings in the last 10 to 15 minutes of the boil. Earlier than that and the long boil breaks the carrageenan down. Later and it may not disperse properly before you start chilling.

Most of the work happens during cooling, when the cold break forms. Chilling fast helps. The colder and quicker the wort cools, the more protein drops out. Our guide to chilling wort fast explains why. After chilling, let the kettle sit for 15 to 20 minutes so the trub settles. Draw clear wort from above it with a siphon or through a tap with a short pickup tube.

More is not better. An overdose produces a fluffy, loose trub that takes up a lot of space at the bottom of the kettle and does not compact. You lose more wort trying to separate it. Follow the maker's dose and adjust only after a few batches.

Dose by volume, not by recipe. A 10 litre batch needs half the finings of a 20 litre one. In a partial boil, dose for the volume actually in the kettle, not the final volume after topping up.
What kettle finings will not fix

Kettle finings target proteins in the wort. They do nothing for yeast that stays in suspension after fermentation, for haze caused by starch from incomplete conversion or for bacterial infection. Each of those needs a different fix.

For yeast haze, time and cold do most of the work. A week at 2 to 4 °C clears many beers. For faster results, gelatine in the fermenter after fermentation is the next step. Our guide to clearing homebrew with gelatine covers it. Brewers of hazy IPAs often still use kettle finings. Protein haze from the kettle is not the same as the haze that defines the style.
Clear beer in a warm climate

Chill haze is the haze that appears when beer goes cold and clears again as it warms. It comes from the same protein and polyphenol complexes that kettle finings target. In India, homebrew often goes from a warm room straight into a cold fridge. Chill haze shows up then.

Kettle finings, a fast chill and a period of cold conditioning together reduce it a lot. Telling one kind of haze from another and tracing it to the step that causes it is part of the troubleshooting we teach on our fundamentals course.
Add finings to your next brew

Put kettle finings on your brew day timeline at 15 minutes before the end of the boil. Buy one packet of tablets or Irish moss and use the maker's dose. Pour a glass of the finished beer after two weeks in the fridge and compare it with your last batch made without them.
faqs: When do I add Irish moss to the boil?
In the last 10 to 15 minutes. Rehydrate it in warm water first so it disperses evenly.
Can kettle finings clear yeast haze?
No. They target proteins in the wort. For yeast haze use cold conditioning or gelatine after fermentation.
Can I use too much Irish moss?
Yes. An overdose gives a fluffy trub that does not compact, so you lose more wort.
